title: AfD and Russian Campaign Pose Threats to Germany's Merz | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Germany confirmed Russia carried out a drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport amid an escalating Russian hybrid-warfare campaign, just as the Russia-friendly AfD polls above 40% ahead of the September 6 Saxony-Anhalt election and Chancellor Merz faces record-low approval (~85% dissatisfaction), together testing whether Germany's political 'firewall' against the far right will hold.

themes.theme: Russian hybrid warfare confirmed and escalating

insights.claim: The German government confirmed on September 1, 2026 that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, in which an airport worker found a drone carrying military-grade explosives near a Ukrainian cargo plane — part of an escalating Russian hybrid campaign against Europe featuring disinformation, drone incursions, cyberwarfare, and sabotage.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: A confirmed state-attributed drone attack targeting Ukraine-linked cargo on German soil is a significant escalation of Russian hybrid warfare inside NATO territory, raising the stakes for how European governments respond without triggering further escalation.

insights.claim: Despite confirming Russian responsibility for the airport attack, Germany's government response has been modest — emphasizing it does not consider itself at war with Russia and announcing primarily diplomatic measures such as closing the Russian consulate general in Bonn — reflecting European leaders' broader caution about responding forcefully out of fear of Russian escalation.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: The gap between confirmed Russian aggression and Germany's muted diplomatic-only response signals European deterrence credibility is being tested in real time — a dynamic likely to embolden further Russian hybrid actions if it continues.

themes.theme: AfD's electoral surge and the 'firewall' question

insights.claim: In the September 6, 2026 Saxony-Anhalt state election, the AfD polls above 40 percent, far ahead of Chancellor Merz's CDU, and a recent national poll found the AfD the most popular party nationally at 28 percent, versus 21 percent for the CDU/CSU and 12 percent for the SPD.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: The AfD leading nationally (28% vs. CDU's 21%) is a landmark shift in German politics that materially raises the risk of the centrist 'firewall' against far-right coalition-building becoming politically unsustainable.

insights.claim: If the AfD performs as strongly as polls suggest in Saxony-Anhalt, it will become challenging for centrist parties to form a government excluding the AfD, and in a worst case the AfD could win an absolute majority, making lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund the first far-right leader of a German state since World War II.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: A Siegmund state-premier win would be a historic marker for post-war German democracy and a concrete near-term event (voting September 6) to watch for confirmation of the AfD firewall's collapse at the state level.

insights.claim: Siegmund's platform centers on deportation as a key electoral issue, a pledge to change the state's history curriculum to de-emphasize the Nazi era in favor of the preceding century, and plans to withdraw the state from the regional public broadcaster — reflecting the AfD's broader radicalization since its 2013 founding from Euroskepticism toward anti-migration, anti-LGBTQ+, anti-climate-policy, and pro-Russia/China positioning.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: The specific curriculum and broadcaster-withdrawal pledges signal an AfD state government would move beyond migration policy into institutional/historical-memory battles, a template to watch for in other German states if the AfD wins power elsewhere.

insights.claim: Germany's domestic intelligence agency classified the AfD as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization in May 2025, though a court provisionally blocked the designation in February 2026 after the party sued; several state branches, including Saxony-Anhalt's, have already been separately designated right-wing extremist.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: The unresolved legal status of the federal extremism designation (blocked pending litigation) means the AfD could win major electoral power in Saxony-Anhalt while its national extremism classification remains legally contested — a governance and legitimacy tension to watch.

themes.theme: Merz's record unpopularity compounds the crisis

insights.claim: Around 85 percent of German voters are dissatisfied with Chancellor Merz's leadership — the highest figure of any chancellor in recent German history — with more than half of his own CDU party's surveyed supporters also disapproving, driven by discontent over slow economic growth and rising energy costs; Merz is particularly unpopular in eastern Germany and among young people.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: Record-low approval even within his own party materially weakens Merz's authority to respond decisively to the Russia hybrid-warfare threat at precisely the moment strong leadership is needed, and raises internal leadership-challenge risk.

insights.claim: Further elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on September 20, 2026 are expected to bring additional AfD gains; a poor showing for Merz's party across these state races, combined with fallout from an already 'mishandled government reshuffle,' could trigger a leadership challenge that would destabilize Germany precisely when it needs to project stability to European and transatlantic partners.
insights.speaker: Liana Fix
insights.so_what: September 20 is a second concrete near-term catalyst after September 6 — a run of AfD gains across both dates would compound pressure toward a CDU leadership crisis just as Germany must respond to Russian hybrid aggression.
